stories.headline: National security calls for collective responsibility: Lt Gen Neeraj Shukla
stories.title: National security calls for collective responsibility: Lt Gen Neeraj Shukla
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: AZARA: National security is not confined to safeguarding the country's borders but also depends on internal stability, social harmony and the collective participation of citizens, Lieutenant General Neeraj Shukla, AVSM, SM, General Officer Commanding (GOC) of Gajraj Corps, said while delivering a special lecture at Gauhati University on Friday.

Speaking on the topic 'Understanding National Security with Special Reference to Northeast India', Lt Gen Shukla said national security was a shared responsibility and not the sole concern of the armed forces.
He emphasised that every citizen had a role to play in building a peaceful, stable and prosperous nation.
Highlighting the importance of national unity and social cohesion, he said these were essential for achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047.
He added that India's security should be viewed from a broader perspective encompassing not only military preparedness but also economic development, social harmony and collective responsibility.

Addressing the students, Lt Gen Shukla said patriotism was reflected not only in the sacrifices and commitment of armed forces personnel guarding the nation's borders but also in the everyday contributions of citizens towards nation-building.
He urged the youth to take pride in India's identity, civilisational heritage and achievements, and contribute to the country's progress through discipline, dedication and a sense of responsibility.

Gauhati University Vice-Chancellor Prof Nani Gopal Mahanta, while addressing the gathering, highlighted the Northeast's rich cultural and linguistic diversity and its integral role in India's national identity.
He said the region's diverse communities, languages and traditions were bound together by a shared sense of belonging and national spirit.
Referring to the Gauhati University anthem composed by Bharat Ratna Dr Bhupen Hazarika, Prof Mahanta said it reflected the region's diversity and the spirit of unity.
He stressed that mutual respect, cultural understanding and social harmony were vital to strengthening national integration.

stories.headline: Assam Government Delays Flood Memorandum Submission Despite Central Visits
stories.title: Assam Government Delays Flood Memorandum Submission Despite Central Visits
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: GUWAHATI: Four months since the devastating flash floods wreaked havoc in the north bank of the Brahmaputra and upper Assam, the state government is yet to submit a flood memorandum to the Centre.
And this is despite two Inter-Ministerial Central Teams (IMCT) visiting Assam twice to assess the flood damage.

In fact, two Central ministers too had visited the state - Shivraj Singh Chauhan had visited Dhemaji district following the flashflood there in June-end, while JP Nadda visited Charaideo and Sivasagar districts to assess damage caused by the devastating flashflood in July.
When a state seeks additional fund from the Centre to cover the damage caused by natural calamities, submission of flood memorandum becomes necessary.
And based on this, IMCTs recommend the Central government to release funds.
But, as per sources, Dispur has failed to submit the flood memorandum till now since the flood damage assessment is yet to be completed.

Opposition legislator Akhil Gogoi has been claiming that huge damage has been caused to houses and other infrastructure, but accused the state government of providing only Rs 15,000 each to some of the affected families.

Due to overall deficit in rainfall, the state did not witness the widespread seasonal floods this year, barring the two flashfloods in Dhemaji and two upper Assam districts of Charaideo and Sivasagar, besides parts of Jorhat district.
But, both the flashfloods caused widespread damage to life and properties.
Over 100 persons lost their lives, while huge damage was causd to houses, roads, rail tracks and bridges.
A railway bridge over the Simen river in Simenchapori area of Dhemaji district collapsed after the turbulent waters of the river eroded the banks, leading to disruption in railway connectivity.

The Dikhari river flowing in from Arunachal Pradesh caused widespread devastation across several villages in Jonai of Dhemaji district during the first wave of flashflood in the north bank of the Brahmaputra.

stories.headline: CRPF DG visits Kulgam attack site, reviews operations as hunt for terrorists enters 3rd day
stories.title: CRPF DG visits Kulgam attack site, reviews operations as hunt for terrorists enters 3rd day
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 13: Director General of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Gyanendra Pratap Singh, on Friday visited the site of the recent terror attack near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district and held detailed interactions with field officers of the CRPF and Jammu and Kashmir Police. The visit came as the joint hunt to track down the attackers entered its third consecutive day, with security forces continuing area-domination and search operations across the south Kashmir belt. During his visit to Kulgam in the Kashmir Valley, the DG CRPF took stock of the ground situation at the attack site in the Nowpora Akhran–Mir Bazar area. He later interacted with field officers of the CRPF and J&K Police at Sadura in Anantnag district, where discussions focused on the way ahead for intensified counter-insurgency (CI) operations in the Valley. The attack, which took place around 2:15 pm on Wednesday, targeted a CRPF checkpoint of the 46th Battalion deployed as a bridge guard roughly two kilometres off the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway. Preliminary investigations have indicated that at least three terrorists were involved, with two believed to be foreign nationals. Three CRPF personnel were injured in the firing. Two have since been discharged after treatment, while the third, who sustained wounds to the abdomen and spine, continues to receive care at the Army’s 92 Base Hospital in Srinagar. On Friday, joint teams of the Army, CRPF and J&K Police maintained an expanded cordon and continued combing operations in the forested and rural stretches around the attack site, while additional searches were underway at multiple locations across south Kashmir. Officials said several suspects were being questioned as part of the investigation, and technical and human intelligence inputs were being analysed to narrow down the movement of the attackers. Continuing his Kashmir Valley tour, Director General CRPF G P Singh, accompanied by senior CRPF officials, visited Head Constable (GD) Sonbir Singh, who is undergoing treatment at Army Hospital, Srinagar. Singh sustained serious injuries while displaying exceptional courage in repulsing a terrorist attack at Nowpora, Akhran in Kulgam on November 11, 2026. The DG CRPF lauded his courage and presence of mind, saying his swift retaliation foiled the terrorists’ designs and averted a major incident. He wished him a speedy recovery and also appreciated the Indian Army for providing prompt helicopter evacuation and quality medical treatment at the Army Hospital.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC: officials
stories.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on sidelines of APEC: officials
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 14: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers. While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs, and they will be heavier in symbolism than substance. Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed on Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries. Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the US war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers. Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly five-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran. The US president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the US war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty -- known as New START -- expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China. But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the US and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With US and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact. Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige. “I would be shocked if there were a joint statement that came out of this meeting that said anything about denuclearisation,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. “I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signalling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," Kagan said. The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades. More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran. The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. “You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said. The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.” Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi. Beijing is the Number one trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022. As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies. In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine. Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan. Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back. Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalised plans for establishing the United Nations. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others. “It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”

stories.headline: J&K retail inflation climbs to 4.88% in October
stories.title: J&K retail inflation climbs to 4.88% in October
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 13: Retail inflation in Jammu and Kashmir accelerated to 4.88 percent in October 2026, up from 4.27 percent in September, extending the upward trend in prices for the sixth consecutive month and adding to the financial burden on households. According to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), inflation in the Union Territory increased by 0.61 percentage points during October. The rate stood at 4.87 percent in rural areas and 4.91 percent in urban areas. The latest reading follows a steady increase in inflation since April, when the rate stood at 2.67 percent. It subsequently rose to 2.84 percent in May, 3.52 percent in June, 3.87 percent in July, 4.09 percent in August and 4.27 percent in September before reaching 4.88 percent in October. The increase in the official inflation rate comes amid concerns over the rising cost of essential commodities and the pressure on household budgets. The rural inflation rate increased from 4.12 percent in September to 4.87 percent in October, marking a rise of 0.75 percentage points. Urban inflation, meanwhile, increased from 4.65 percent to 4.91 percent during the same period. The figures indicate that rural areas witnessed a sharper acceleration in inflation than urban areas, although the overall rate remained marginally higher in urban areas. Despite the increase, J&K’s inflation rate remained below the national average of 6.09 percent in October. India’s retail inflation rose from 5.54 percent in September to 6.09 percent in October. Nationally, rural inflation stood at 6.63 percent, while urban inflation was recorded at 5.41 percent. At the national level, food inflation, measured through the Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI), increased to 8.94 percent in October from 7.74 percent in September, indicating mounting pressure from food prices. Among individual commodities nationally, onion prices registered an annual increase of 116.22 percent, while garlic prices rose by 60.74 percent. Ginger and lemon prices increased by 48.32 percent and 47.30 percent, respectively. In contrast, potato prices declined by 14.24 percent and cauliflower prices fell by 10.57 percent. The national CPI data also showed that restaurants and accommodation services recorded inflation of 10.06 percent, while personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services registered inflation of 10.14 percent. However, these commodity-wise and category-wise figures are national estimates and do not represent individual inflation rates for Jammu and Kashmir. The October CPI figures are provisional and are based on the revised CPI series with 2024 as the base year. The National Statistics Office collected price data from 1,407 selected urban markets, including online markets, and 1,465 villages across the country. The CPI for November 2026 is scheduled to be released on December 14.

stories.headline: Ten Years After the Note Ban
stories.title: Ten Years After the Note Ban
stories.summary: On 8th November 2016 at 8 o’clock in the evening, the Prime Minister announced that ₹500 and ₹1000 notes would become invalid from midnight. These notes constituted around 86% of the currency. Ten years later, we take a serious look at how well the policy met its objectives. Black Money The government had three objectives to achieve: remove black money, remove fake notes and remove terror funding. It later became a reason to increase digitisation. Its main aim was to utilise the fact that black money is mostly kept in cash and therefore would have to be deposited as it would be exposed. However, the Reserve Bank of India annual report shows that out of ₹15.41 lakh crore of specific notes in circulation, ₹15.31 lakh crore (99.3%) were returned. This suggests that there was very little cash in circulation that hadn’t been declared or more likely there was some laundering done. Economists have always argued that black money is mostly kept in property, gold and foreign assets. Therefore, swapping the currency was never going to be effective. The state also had high costs. The RBI had to print ₹7965 crore in 2016-17 compared to 2015-16 which was ₹3421 crore. It also increased to ₹4912 crore in 2017-18. Fake Notes and Terror Funding In 2017-18 fake notes were detected down by 31.4% to 5.22 lakh. However, in 2024-25, 2.17 lakh were detected. Fake notes aren’t easy to attribute, but it is true that there has been a decrease. There have been some fake notes of the new ₹500 design. These increased by 37.3% to 1.18 lakh in 2024-25. Terror funding is difficult to verify. The onus was on the policy maker to prove their point. Digitisation This is the best reason to support the policy. However, it is the least causal. The UPI was launched on 25th August 2016. In 2016-17 there were 1.78 crore transactions, however this increased to 24162 crore in 2025-26. The value of these transactions increased from ₹0.07 lakh crore to around ₹314 lakh crore. This is due to the fact that there is a lot of interoperability in public infrastructure. The Note Ban just gave a push to this. However, there was an increase in the amount of money in circulation. At the end of 2025-26, there was ₹41.68 lakh crore in circulation. This was more than double what there was ten years ago. The increase was 11.9% in 2025-26. This was the highest increase since 2017-18 when there was a recovery after the Note Ban. This increase was partly caused by increased consumption, lower interest rates and the fact that ₹2000 notes were replaced. India has become more digitised. GDP Growth GDP growth in the first quarter of 2016-17 decreased to 7.5%, 7.0% and 6.1%. Supporters argue that the full year was later revised to show an increase to 8.3% and the RBI acknowledged that there was a slowdown in the first quarter of 2016-17. This is true, however, you should be cautious about saying there was a precise decrease in output. The data isn’t great to look at. Critics argue that the informal sector is the largest part of the economy to use cash and is estimated using the national accounts. These are mostly estimated using the formal sector as a basis. This could mean that there wasn’t as big of a shock as there could have been. There was a decrease in growth in 2017-18 and 2018-19. This was due to a number of factors including the Note Ban and the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax. This seems like a reasonable argument. However, there isn’t much evidence to show that there wasn’t already a trend. There isn’t evidence to show that this was genuine cash. By March 2018 the amount of money in circulation had increased beyond the amount before the Note Ban. A reasonable argument could be made that there could have been a more targeted approach using enforcement, analytics and incentives to increase the amount of cash in the formal sector. Legality A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court ruled on 2nd January 2023 that the decision was legal (4-1). The majority argued that there was a reasonable connection between the aims of the policy and that it passed the test of proportionality. They also argued that the courts should stay out of economic policy. The minority opinion was given by Justice B.V. Nagarathna who argued that the action was ‘vitiated and unlawful’. This is due to the fact that the action shouldn’t have been taken in a Gazette Notification and should have been done through legislation. She also argues that the RBI didn’t give independent consideration to the action. There were long queues, quarterly growth slowed and there were high printing costs. We can learn that surprise isn’t the way to go. A policy that involves 86% of the currency by value should be rolled out in stages and there should be plenty of replacement notes. We can also learn that it is important to involve the right institutions. The RBI should have a clear and meaningful role in the process. Finally, any large economic intervention should have clear metrics and independent evaluation. This means that in ten years’ time we will be debating the evidence rather than the inference. The biggest legacy of the Note Ban may be the lack of evidence. Malik Daniyal is a regular contributor to GK.

stories.headline: Assam Government to Seek Supreme Court Nod for Full NRC Revision Amid Political Debate
stories.title: Assam Government to Seek Supreme Court Nod for Full NRC Revision Amid Political Debate
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: GUWAHATI: Seven years after publication of the final list, the ghost of National Register of Citizens (NRC) seems to have come to haunt Assam once again.

With Dispur now opting for a complete revision of the final NRC before the Supreme Court, the issue has seemingly transformed into a contentious topic, sparking a renewed political debate in the state.

And with leading groups and organisations also joining the cacophony, the issue is likely to keep the state's political pot boiling in the coming days, especially since there is no unanimity among the stakeholders over the issue.

While the Government of Assam is ready to knock on the doors of the country's apex court to seek a full revision of the NRC, influential groups like the All Assam Students' Union (AASU) also demanded a review but stopped short of saying whether it wanted a full overhaul or only partial.
Even Dispur had earlier stated that it would seek a revision of 20% of the names included in the final NRC in the state's border areas and 10% in the rest.
But now it has changed its mind by seeking a full revision.
Taking an opposite stand, the Congress party has stated that since the final NRC was published in 2019, it should now be implemented.

The Assam Pradesh Congress Committee (APCC) on Friday demanded that the central and state governments clarify the status of the NRC, complete the pending process and issue citizenship identity documents to the 3.11 crore people included in the final list published in 2019.

Former MLAs and senior Congress spokespersons Binanda Saikia and Satyabrata Kalita, along with Assam Pradesh Mahila Congress president Mira Borthakur Goswami, questioned the government's silence over the NRC despite the passage of more than seven years since the final list was published on August 31, 2019.

Alleging that the BJP had used the NRC and the issue of illegal foreigners as election promises but subsequently abandoned the matter, Saikia demanded a clear timeline for completing the remaining work.
He also claimed that nearly three lakh indigenous people were among those excluded.
Kalita said more than Rs 1,600 crore was spent on the NRC exercise, involving around 55,000 employees, but the process had remained incomplete.

stories.headline: Div Com orders snow clearance, advance stocking in remote areas; 4x4 ambulances, 24x7 control rooms for winter
stories.title: Div Com orders snow clearance, advance stocking in remote areas; 4x4 ambulances, 24x7 control rooms for winter
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 13: Divisional Commissioner Kashmir Anshul Garg on Friday directed departments to ensure prompt snow clearance, advance stocking of essential commodities in remote areas and uninterrupted essential services as part of winter preparedness across Kashmir Division. Chairing a high-level meeting, Garg stressed coordinated efforts and timely response to minimise public inconvenience during the winter season. The meeting was attended by Deputy Commissioners, Commissioner Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC), Director Airport Authority Srinagar, SSP Traffic Rural and senior officers from KPDCL, R&B, MED, PMGSY, ULB, BRO, NHAI, Irrigation and Flood Control, PHE, IMD, FCS&CA, Health, SDA, Police and other concerned departments. Reviewing snow clearance action plans, the Divisional Commissioner directed MED, R&B, PMGSY, ULB, SMC and BRO to ensure prompt clearance of snow and clearly demarcate jurisdictional responsibilities to avoid duplication and confusion. He stressed optimal utilisation of available machinery and manpower and directed agencies to complete all pending stage contracts to strengthen the snow clearance mechanism. Chief Engineers and other officers informed the meeting that adequate arrangements were in place to ensure timely snow clearance on highways, major roads, streets and inner lanes immediately after snowfall. Reviewing winter power preparedness, Garg assessed electricity demand and supply, availability of buffer stocks of transformers, transformer oil, DG sets and HSD in Gurez, besides the status of branch cutting. The meeting was informed that all districts had adequate transformer stocks and 80 percent of branch cutting had been completed. It was further informed that average electricity demand in the Valley during winter was around 1,700 MW against an average supply of 1,300 MW, while peak demand touched 2,400 MW. The Divisional Commissioner directed the Chief Engineer, KPDCL, to augment workshop capacity wherever required, complete the remaining branch-cutting work at the earliest, strictly adhere to scheduled power curtailment timings and ensure prompt repair of damaged transformers. Reviewing the availability of essential commodities in remote and snowbound areas, including Gurez and the Karnah-Machil-Keran belt, he directed FCS&CA to complete advance stocking of LPG, petroleum products, rice and wheat within a week. He stressed that adequate stocks be maintained in all far-flung areas to prevent shortages and inconvenience to the public during road closures. Taking note of delays in the commencement of winter air sorties in Bandipora and Kupwara, Garg directed the Civil Aviation Department to operationalise the facility by December 1 to facilitate emergency transportation from remote and inaccessible areas. Regarding flight operations at Srinagar Airport, he directed the Director, Airport Authority Srinagar, to ensure timely dissemination of information to passengers and the general public about changes in flight schedules due to adverse weather conditions. The Divisional Commissioner also reviewed healthcare preparedness across districts, including heating arrangements in hospitals, availability of essential medicines, deployment of medical staff in far-flung areas and the requirement for 4x4 ambulances. He directed the National Health Mission (NHM) to provide 4x4 ambulances to the Directorate of Health Services Kashmir for distribution among districts, in addition to SANJY ambulances. Emphasising proactive healthcare arrangements, Garg directed the Health Department to undertake comprehensive line-listing of expectant mothers and critically ill patients in vulnerable and remote areas. He also stressed advance shifting of such patients to temporary shelters, wherever required, to ensure uninterrupted access to medical care during heavy snowfall and road closures. Reviewing the preparedness of the Jal Shakti Department, he directed officials to ensure uninterrupted functioning of all PHE schemes, including lift water supply schemes, and make adequate arrangements for deploying water tankers wherever required to ensure drinking water availability. He also directed the Forest Department to ensure adequate stocking of firewood at depots across the Valley. To strengthen interdepartmental coordination, Garg directed all district administrations and departments to ensure round-the-clock functioning of their respective control rooms, including the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC). He also instructed departments to appoint nodal officers and share their contact details to facilitate timely assistance, coordination and dissemination of information. Stressing the importance of timely weather-related advisories, he directed concerned departments to promptly share weather and avalanche forecasts with the public to minimise risks and safeguard lives. Meanwhile, he directed the Commissioner, SMC, to identify waterlogging hotspots across Srinagar city and ensure deployment of adequate dewatering pumps to address any eventuality during winter. The Divisional Commissioner also emphasised accountability and timely grievance redressal, directing officers to properly document the time of occurrence of any issue and the response time taken by the concerned department to resolve it. During the meeting, Deputy Commissioners briefed the chair about winter preparedness measures undertaken in their respective districts and highlighted critical issues requiring intervention and resolution. Garg called upon all departments to maintain close coordination and ensure that necessary arrangements were put in place well in advance to minimise public inconvenience and ensure the safety and well-being of people across Kashmir Division during the winter season.

stories.headline: Beyond Blood Sugar
stories.title: Beyond Blood Sugar
stories.summary: Diabetes, known since antiquity, was described by Sushruta in 6th-century BCE in India as Madhumeha. The Greek physician Apollonius coined the term diabetes around 250 BCE, while Thomas Willis added mellitus in 1675. Insulin’s discovery by Banting and Best in 1921 revolutionised treatment, earning them the 1923 Nobel Prize. Today, diabetes is a global epidemic. Diabetes mellitus is broadly categorized into two main forms: Type 1, resulting from the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, and Type 2, driven by impaired insulin secretion and cellular insulin resistance. Though Type 1 diabetes starts at relatively young ages like children, adolescents and young adults and Type II in Middle Ages around 45 years but there are no real cut offs. The key is an early recognition. The World Health Organization in a study of worldwide trends in diabetes prevalence and treatment from 1990 to 2022 estimates that diabetes will be the 7th leading cause of death. In India in 2023, a report by the ICMR on Metabolic and non-communicable diseases data highlighted an overall weighted prevalence of 11.4% (Jammu region 18.9 %) alongside a prediabetes prevalence of 15.3% (Jammu region 10.8%). As per the updated National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) across the combined Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, (2023-24) survey reported that 13% of women and 11.3% of men aged 15 and above in Jammu and Kashmir have elevated blood sugar levels or are taking medication for diabetes. To confront this growing crisis, World Diabetes Day is observed annually on November 14th coinciding with the date of birth of Sir Fredrick Banting. The campaign theme this year emphasizes “Early action on diabetes,” underscoring the critical need for earlier diagnosis, expanded access to comprehensive care, and the reduction of social stigma. It is alarming that according to a global health data published by the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) and analytical medical research organizations 40% of individuals with diabetes remain undiagnosed. This proportion is likely to be even higher in our Indian settings. Early diagnosis hinges on public awareness of classic symptoms: excessive thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), unexplained fatigue and weakness, and rapid weight loss despite a good appetite. Recommended screening milestones include a basic blood sugar check where every individual should know their baseline levels—in a healthy adult, fasting blood sugar should ideally be below 100 mg/dL, and random samples (2 hours post meal) should remain under 140 mg/dL as per the American Diabetic Association (ADA) 2026 guidelines. Those ADA recommends a blood sugar estimation at age 35 years regardless of weight. However, in persons with a higher risk overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² or >85th percentile for youth) and have additional risk factors such as: Family history of diabetes, High-risk race or ethnicity, like us in India, history of gestational diabetes, Conditions associated with insulin resistance (such as polycystic ovary syndrome or high blood pressure), screening should start at in youth/ adolescence starting at age 10 years or the onset of puberty. Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c). Timely diagnosis is only valuable when paired with accessible, affordable care and sustained lifestyle integration. Effective management requires a collaborative, multi-disciplinary approach: Lifestyle Optimization: Adopt a healthy diet low in refined carbohydrates and sugars, rich in seasonal fruits, vegetables, and fibre. Combine this with regular physical activity—aiming for more than 8,000 steps per day at least 5 days a week, supplemented by strengthening exercises for a minimum of 2 hours per week—and absolute avoidance of tobacco in any form. These foundational steps reduce reliance on medications. Pharmacological and Clinical Targets: Modern therapeutics effectively minimize the risk of heart failure, heart attacks, and strokes. For established diabetics, maintaining glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) levels close to 6.5% to 7% is paramount. Comprehensive Vascular Protection: Blood sugar control must be coupled with keeping blood pressure at or below 130/80 mm Hg and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels below 70 mg/dL. Many essential medications are readily available as high-efficacy, low-cost generics manufactured by reputable Indian pharmaceutical companies. Environmental and Policy Support: Curbing Type 2 diabetes requires healthier community environments, calling for active contributions from health, urban planning, and rural development ministries to ensure universal access to healthy food, safe recreational spaces, and quality health services. Beyond the physiological toll, individuals with diabetes frequently face psychological burdens due to social stigma. Well-meaning family members and peers often attribute the condition to poor dietary self-indulgence, lack of willpower, or sheer carelessness. This social pressure frequently drives patients into secrecy: avoiding insulin injections or skipping blood glucose monitoring in public or social gatherings. Left unaddressed, this cycle fosters denial, anxiety, and depressive states, which ultimately compromises metabolic control and accelerates complications. The paradigm shift needed requires empathetic counselling, ensuring patients are counselled that diabetes is a complex metabolic disorder shaped by intricate genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors—it is never a personal failure. Treating physicians should provide compassionate clinical care by dedicating adequate time to educate patients thoroughly without inducing fear. The message of acceptance must be clear and unwavering: diabetes is nothing to be ashamed of, but simply a condition to be understood, accepted, and effectively managed. Conclusion: The battle against diabetes cannot be won by medicines and medical interventions alone. It requires a collective commitment involving individuals, families, healthcare professionals, communities and policymakers. We must move from a reactive approach, where treatment begins after the disease is detected, to a proactive way of prevention, early screening and sustained health awareness. Equally important is the need to replace judgement with empathy and stigma with understanding. No individual should ever feel embarrassed or discriminated against for living with diabetes. Humanity has travelled a remarkable journey from recognizing the sweetness of urine in ancient India to discovering insulin and developing sophisticated therapies by a joint effort so that we can prevent life-threatening complications. Yet, despite these extraordinary scientific advances, the real challenge remains ensuring that their benefits reach every individual. Our ultimate goal should not merely be to help people live with diabetes, but to prevent diabetes wherever possible and enable those affected to live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives. Early awareness, timely action and compassionate care must become the cornerstones of this global fight. Author is Founder Director, Gauri Kaul Foundation

opening: Diabetes, known since antiquity, was described by Sushruta in 6th-century BCE in India as Madhumeha.
The Greek physician Apollonius coined the term diabetes around 250 BCE, while Thomas Willis added mellitus in 1675.
body: Insulin’s discovery by Banting and Best in 1921 revolutionised treatment, earning them the 1923 Nobel Prize.
Today, diabetes is a global epidemic.

Diabetes mellitus is broadly categorized into two main forms: Type 1, resulting from the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, and Type 2, driven by impaired insulin secretion and cellular insulin resistance.
Though Type 1 diabetes starts at relatively young ages like children, adolescents and young adults and Type II in Middle Ages around 45 years but there are no real cut offs.
The key is an early recognition.
The World Health Organization in a study of worldwide trends in diabetes prevalence and treatment from 1990 to 2022 estimates that diabetes will be the 7th leading cause of death.

In India in 2023, a report by the ICMR on Metabolic and non-communicable diseases data highlighted an overall weighted prevalence of 11.4% (Jammu region 18.9 %) alongside a prediabetes prevalence of 15.3% (Jammu region 10.8%).

As per the updated National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) across the combined Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, (2023-24) survey reported that 13% of women and 11.3% of men aged 15 and above in Jammu and Kashmir have elevated blood sugar levels or are taking medication for diabetes.
To confront this growing crisis, World Diabetes Day is observed annually on November 14th coinciding with the date of birth of Sir Fredrick Banting.
The campaign theme this year emphasizes “Early action on diabetes,” underscoring the critical need for earlier diagnosis, expanded access to comprehensive care, and the reduction of social stigma.
This proportion is likely to be even higher in our Indian settings.

Early diagnosis hinges on public awareness of classic symptoms: excessive thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), unexplained fatigue and weakness, and rapid weight loss despite a good appetite.

Recommended screening milestones include a basic blood sugar check where every individual should know their baseline levels—in a healthy adult, fasting blood sugar should ideally be below 100 mg/dL, and random samples (2 hours post meal) should remain under 140 mg/dL as per the American Diabetic Association (ADA) 2026 guidelines.
Those ADA recommends a blood sugar estimation at age 35 years regardless of weight.

However, in persons with a higher risk overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² or >85th percentile for youth) and have additional risk factors such as: Family history of diabetes, High-risk race or ethnicity, like us in India, history of gestational diabetes, Conditions associated with insulin resistance (such as polycystic ovary syndrome or high blood pressure), screening should start at in youth/ adolescence starting at age 10 years or the onset of puberty.
Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c).
Timely diagnosis is only valuable when paired with accessible, affordable care and sustained lifestyle integration.

Effective management requires a collaborative, multi-disciplinary approach: Lifestyle Optimization: Adopt a healthy diet low in refined carbohydrates and sugars, rich in seasonal fruits, vegetables, and fibre.

Combine this with regular physical activity—aiming for more than 8,000 steps per day at least 5 days a week, supplemented by strengthening exercises for a minimum of 2 hours per week—and absolute avoidance of tobacco in any form.
These foundational steps reduce reliance on medications.
Pharmacological and Clinical Targets: Modern therapeutics effectively minimize the risk of heart failure, heart attacks, and strokes.
For established diabetics, maintaining glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) levels close to 6.5% to 7% is paramount.
Comprehensive Vascular Protection: Blood sugar control must be coupled with keeping blood pressure at or below 130/80 mm Hg and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels below 70 mg/dL.
Many essential medications are readily available as high-efficacy, low-cost generics manufactured by reputable Indian pharmaceutical companies.

Environmental and Policy Support: Curbing Type 2 diabetes requires healthier community environments, calling for active contributions from health, urban planning, and rural development ministries to ensure universal access to healthy food, safe recreational spaces, and quality health services.
Beyond the physiological toll, individuals with diabetes frequently face psychological burdens due to social stigma.
Well-meaning family members and peers often attribute the condition to poor dietary self-indulgence, lack of willpower, or sheer carelessness.
This social pressure frequently drives patients into secrecy: avoiding insulin injections or skipping blood glucose monitoring in public or social gatherings.
Left unaddressed, this cycle fosters denial, anxiety, and depressive states, which ultimately compromises metabolic control and accelerates complications.

The paradigm shift needed requires empathetic counselling, ensuring patients are counselled that diabetes is a complex metabolic disorder shaped by intricate genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors—it is never a personal failure.
Treating physicians should provide compassionate clinical care by dedicating adequate time to educate patients thoroughly without inducing fear.
The message of acceptance must be clear and unwavering: diabetes is nothing to be ashamed of, but simply a condition to be understood, accepted, and effectively managed.
Conclusion: The battle against diabetes cannot be won by medicines and medical interventions alone.
It requires a collective commitment involving individuals, families, healthcare professionals, communities and policymakers.
We must move from a reactive approach, where treatment begins after the disease is detected, to a proactive way of prevention, early screening and sustained health awareness.
Equally important is the need to replace judgement with empathy and stigma with understanding.
No individual should ever feel embarrassed or discriminated against for living with diabetes.

Humanity has travelled a remarkable journey from recognizing the sweetness of urine in ancient India to discovering insulin and developing sophisticated therapies by a joint effort so that we can prevent life-threatening complications.
Yet, despite these extraordinary scientific advances, the real challenge remains ensuring that their benefits reach every individual.
Our ultimate goal should not merely be to help people live with diabetes, but to prevent diabetes wherever possible and enable those affected to live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives.
Early awareness, timely action and compassionate care must become the cornerstones of this global fight.
Author is Founder Director, Gauri Kaul Foundation.

article_sentences: Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy LIVE — Follow live updates, score and highlights for the first round of SMAT 2026, with Jharkhand starting as defending champion.
Anukul Roy will lead Jharkhand as it begins its title defence in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy on Saturday.
Welcome to Sportstar’s live coverage of the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2026, being held across 19 venues in India, with defending champion Jharkhand taking on Mizoram.
Follow this space for live updates as and when they come.
The latest edition of SMAT will get underway on November 14, with thirty-eight teams competing for the title, with the final scheduled on December 6.
With less than a month until the IPL 2027 auction, the competition offers novice players the chance to get the attention of IPL scouts and experienced combatants the chance to improve.
Haryana, the runner-up from the previous season, will play Punjab, while Jharkhand, the reigning champion, will start its campaign against Mizoram, the 2025 plate group winner.
Railways will take on Tamil Nadu, the tournament’s most successful team with three titles.
